title: The administrative record and contemporaneous reasons
shortTitle: The administrative record and contemporaneous reasons
summary: The administrative record contains the material before the agency when it acted; review ordinarily evaluates the grounds the agency actually invoked.
notes:
Overton Park’s record requirement affects agency organization: officials anticipating review must assemble information and explain decisions in a way a court can examine. The remand history also shows that record-based review applies when an agency later refuses approval; the Sixth Circuit ultimately rejected a demand that the Secretary identify a particular alternative route before refusing the park route. The editors question how a model of explicit findings captures intergovernmental bargaining and evolving planning.

Chenery’s principle protects the agency’s delegated responsibility: a reviewing court should not adopt a new policy rationale that the agency never selected. Additional explanation may clarify an existing rationale, but supplying a distinct new ground ordinarily requires new agency action. Regents applies that distinction to an agency official’s later memorandum as well as a lawyer’s litigation argument. Department of Commerce adds a distinct issue: an explanation can be facially plausible yet contrived. Exceptional evidence of pretext may justify inquiry beyond the record, while disagreement with policy alone does not warrant routine exploration of motives.
